headline: Tesla Roadster flies and drives upside down, with SpaceX thrusters and suction system
summary: The next-gen Tesla Roadster was unveiled with wild stunts, including driving upside down and hovering. Its 'Thrust' package, featuring SpaceX-derived cold-gas thrusters and a suction system, costs an additional $245,000.
details: Tesla has officially unveiled the next-generation Roadster, nine years after its concept prototype was first shown. The reveal event at the SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, featured the vehicle performing incredible stunts, including driving upside down on a C-shaped ramp.

During the unveiling, the Roadster also jumped off the ramp, flipped, and used its thruster system to safely hover to the ground. An Optimus robot was seated in the driver's seat for show, with the stunts pre-programmed into the vehicle.

Tesla explained that the car's ability to stick upside down to the ramp is due to a multi-mode fan and ground sealing system. This system pulls air from beneath the vehicle, generating downforce and suction.

The vehicle's jump and controlled landing are powered by attitude-control thrusters and rear thrusters, which incorporate technology from SpaceX. These advanced cold-gas thrusters use all-electric actuators for precise, micro-second adjustments.

While initial pre-orders for the Roadster began years ago, new reservations require a $5,000 deposit, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days for the base model. The 'Thrust' package, which includes the suction system and acceleration thrusters, demands an extra $245,000 within 10 days of reservation.
The full-flight 'Rocket' version of the Roadster is an invite-only offering, suggesting it will be an even more exclusive and high-performance variant.

headline_marked: [[Meta to scrape business websites]] starting Oct. 30, affecting news publishers
headline: Meta to scrape business websites starting Oct. 30, affecting news publishers
summary: New commercial terms, effective October 30, allow Meta to crawl and collect content from websites associated with business accounts, including news publishers, potentially for AI training. There is no opt-out option for businesses.
details: Meta's updated commercial terms, effective October 30, grant the company permission to crawl and collect content from websites "associated with" business accounts on its platforms. This broad update impacts various companies, including news publishers who manage Facebook pages, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels.

Legal experts reviewing the terms suggest Meta could use this content to train its AI products, potentially accessing material that would otherwise cost millions in licensing. The terms explicitly state content from such domains can be used to "train" and "develop" Meta Company Products, which include "AI at Meta."

Cornell Law professor James Grimmelmann notes this could give Meta permission to train AI on publishers' content and potentially deploy it in competition, or even develop a comprehensive archive. He describes it as an "astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions" if fully enforced.

Crucially, there is no opt-out option for business accounts ahead of October 30; businesses must either agree to the terms or cease using Meta's products for commercial purposes. Meta claims this language consolidates existing terms and that robots.txt can still manage crawler access.

However, legal experts argue the new commercial terms might supersede robots.txt instructions, and the update also allows Meta to create "test credentials" to access websites. Publishers are advised to assume the terms are enforceable.
